title: Key organizer of Pearson gold heist says his money was taken during kidnapping in Pakistan

image.caption: Archit Grover is expected to face trial in November 2027. (Peel Regional Police)

blocks.text: Arsalan Chaudhary, who is serving four years in prison for his role in the Pearson Airport gold heist, began testifying Tuesday at the trial of former Air Canada employee Parmpal Sidhu, who is facing charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.

items: Arsalan Chaudhary, a man serving four years in prison for his role in the 2023 Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist, testified Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu. Chaudhary, who will return to the witness box Wednesday, said that the planning of the heist was "all me."

Chaudhary said he melted some of the stolen gold and received $200,000 to $300,000 for it, then travelled to Pakistan. He said he was subsequently kidnapped and abused, and when he was released the money was gone.

Sidhu is a former Air Canada employee accused of providing a doctored document that allowed for the pickup of more than $22 million in gold and currency. Sidhu pleaded not guilty earlier this month to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.
Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.
Sidhu's trial, which began in a Brampton, Ont., courtroom on Oct. 5, is before Justice Gordon Cudjoe.

blocks.text: What we learned from Tuesday's testimony
What the 'mastermind' of the $22M Pearson gold heist had to say in court

Arsalan Chaudhary, currently serving a four-year sentence for his role in the $22-million Toronto Pearson airport heist, testified Tuesday in the trial of a former Air Canada employee. Parmpal Sidhu, the former employee, is accused of altering cargo documents to enable the massive theft of gold and cash.
It was a stuffy, packed courtroom proceeding Tuesday in the trial for Parmpal Sidhu, for his alleged involvement in the 2023 Pearson airport gold heist.

Crown prosecutors previously alleged in court that Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson cargo bay.

Arsalan Chaudhary, the 43-year-old believed to have been at the helm of the operation, testified during Sidhu's trial Tuesday. He told the Brampton Ont., court that the "planning of the gold heist was all me" and that he had "heard" of Sidhu but doesn't "really know him."

Chaudhary remained vague in his description of Sidhu, and his testimony was muddled, interrupting Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic numerous times and prompting Justice Gordon Cudjoe to tell him to "take a deep breath" before answering more questions.

Most of Chaudhary's testimony Tuesday focused on text and group chat messages related to the heist that he said he did not remember or recall. His testimony also shed light on what he did with the portion of gold that he took for himself.
According to his testimony, Chaudhary took a third of the gold from the heist and stashed it in a condo in the Greater Toronto Area. He melted it for sale, acquiring $200,000 to $300,000 in cash.
He eventually made his way to Pakistan with the money, where he said he was abducted and forced to give it up, along with the remaining gold from the condo unit in Canada.
Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

October 13Defence lawyer says case is 'looking good'Meagan FitzpatrickSidhu walked out of the courthouse with his lawyers and while he declined to comment on Chaudhary’s testimony so far, one of his lawyers made brief remarks. Shale Wagman said they are keeping an “open mind” about the case and there is more evidence to come but “so far it’s looking good.” When asked to elaborate, Wagman said he hasn’t heard anything bad against his client.

Chaudhary to continue testifying tomorrowAlina SnisarenkoWe have just learned that there appears to be a scheduling conflict for this afternoon. So instead of us breaking for lunch, it's actually for the rest of the day.Sidhu's trial will continue tomorrow with Chaudhary resuming his testimony. Chaudhary was just escorted out of the witness box by a special constable with Peel police, and I just stepped out along with everyone else for the day.

Chaudhary continues struggling to recall timeline of eventsAlina SnisarenkoArchit Grover is expected to face trial in November 2027. (Peel Regional Police)Vlacic has reviewed two more exhibits with Chaudhary, which were papers that depict names or letters and monetary values next to them in a list format. While Chaudhary admitted to writing one of the lists at first, he later had trouble recalling whether the pieces of paper shown were familiar to him.He said he made a "fake" list for his kidnappers in Pakistan to "show them that I have no money left, everything is done." He also said the first list "looks more familiar" to him, but couldn't recall the second list Vlacic presented. He later said the second piece of paper was a copy of the list he made. One of the names on the list is Archit Grover. When asked if he knew him, Chaudhary said they were "good friends" who ran in the "same circle." Chaudhary said he co-ordinated with Grover to get access to a truck through his trucking company. The truck and the driver were both from his company, he said. He said he did not let Grover know that he was picking up stolen gold. Grover is expected to stand trial for his alleged involvement in the gold heist next fall.

Judge asks Chaudhary to 'take a deep breath'Alina SnisarenkoAs Vlacic continued her examination, she asked Chaudhary more questions about his phone activity and messages. Chaudhary appeared a bit agitated, continuously saying no to her. After interrupting Vlacic a couple times, Judge Gordon Cudjoe paused Vlacic's examination to tell Chaudhary to "take a deep breath" and let her finish before answering.Chaudhary apologized.
We're back from breakAlina SnisarenkoI'm back in the courtroom after a 15-minute break. Chaudhary is still in the witness box, and Vlacic is resuming her examination.

Court proceedings paused for breakAlina SnisarenkoJudge Gordon Cudjoe has just paused Vlacic's examination, signalling time for break. Everyone was asked to leave the courtroom. Vlacic will continue her examination in 15 minutes.

Crown asking Chaudhary about text messagesAlina SnisarenkoThe Superior Court of Justice in Brampton, Ont., in 2024. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)As his testimony continued, Vlacic provided Chaudhary with a cell phone number and asked Chaudhary to verify it was his. He didn't outright say it was his or who the number belonged to.Vlacic asked him questions about a specific phone contact named Jazz. He said he can't recall having that contact.The Crown is reviewing numerous messages with that contact. Chaudhary said he doesn't recall any of the conversations and whether he participated in them. The conversations depict planning around truck unloading and driver availability.Chaudhary said he does not recall the conversations or what they pertain to. He said he has "no clue" whether these messages were on his phone, at times vigorously shaking his head no.

Chaudhary details Pakistan kidnappingAlina SnisarenkoChaudhary provided some more details on his kidnapping in Pakistan, saying that he "didn't know what the f--k was going on." He told Crown attorney Vlacic that when his kidnappers released him, the gold heist money he had with him while he was in the country was gone.When asked how he felt about it, Chaudhary said he was "lucky to be alive."He declined to provide details of what treatment he received, at first noting his kidnappers administered electrical shock to him, but then stopping short and asking to skip the question."I wanted to get the f out of Pakistan," he said. He said he flew to Dubai afterwards.

Chaudhary says he had 'no plan' for stolen goldAlina SnisarenkoChaudhary said after he melted the gold he got his "friend to take it to a jewelry shop where I got cash for it." He said he got around $200,000 to $300,000 for it. When asked what his plan was with money from the gold, he said he didn't have one. At one point, he admitted to going abroad to Pakistan, saying he wanted to invest the money and "buy a business or something."
